etiquette.title: Be punctual — always
etiquette.tip: Punctuality is a sign of respect in Germany. Aim to arrive 5 minutes early for meetings; if you'll be even slightly late, send a quick message.

etiquette.title: Use 'Sie' and surnames first
etiquette.tip: Address colleagues as 'Sie' with Herr/Frau + surname (and Dr./Prof. titles in academia) until they offer the informal 'du'. Let the senior person or host offer 'du' first.

etiquette.title: A firm, brief handshake
etiquette.tip: Shake hands with a firm grip and direct eye contact when meeting someone, and often again when leaving. Greet the room when you enter ('Guten Tag').

etiquette.title: Directness isn't rudeness
etiquette.tip: Germans value honest, direct communication. Frank feedback is meant constructively, not personally — and they'll appreciate clear, straightforward answers from you too.

etiquette.title: Quiet Sundays (Ruhetag)
etiquette.tip: Sundays are rest days: most shops are closed and loud activities (drilling, loud music) are frowned upon. Buy groceries by Saturday.

etiquette.title: Recycling is taken seriously
etiquette.tip: Separate your waste: paper, packaging (Gelber Sack), glass (by color), bio, and residual. Bottles/cans often have a deposit (Pfand) — return them at the supermarket machine.

etiquette.title: Carry cash
etiquette.tip: Many cafés, bakeries and smaller shops are cash-only or have a card minimum. Keep some euros and coins on you, especially for lunch.

etiquette.title: Wait for the green man
etiquette.tip: Crossing on a red pedestrian light is frowned upon — especially with children around. Just wait; it's a small but noticed courtesy.

etiquette.title: Always have a valid ticket
etiquette.tip: On trams and buses, validate your ticket and keep it. Ticket controls are frequent and fare-dodging ('Schwarzfahren') brings an on-the-spot fine.

etiquette.title: Eye contact when you toast
etiquette.tip: When clinking glasses ('Prost!'), look the other person in the eye — skipping it is considered bad luck and a bit rude.

etiquette.title: Respect 'Feierabend'
etiquette.tip: The end of the workday and free time are respected. Don't expect work replies in the evening or on weekends, and enjoy your own downtime too.

etiquette.title: Show genuine interest in sustainability
etiquette.tip: Environmental topics matter deeply here — and especially at DBFZ. Curiosity about their research and Germany's energy transition (Energiewende) goes a long way.

gifts.title: Paçoca / Pacoquinha — great choice!
gifts.note: A peanut sweet is uniquely Brazilian and easy to share. Bring a box/pack for the whole team rather than one person, present it modestly, and mention it contains peanuts (Erdnüsse) for anyone with allergies. Don't expect it to be opened in front of you.

gifts.title: Brazilian coffee
gifts.note: Brazilian coffee is well regarded and a natural conversation starter with German colleagues, who take coffee seriously. A nice bag of specialty beans is always welcome.

gifts.title: Other regional sweets
gifts.note: Brigadeiro, pé-de-moleque, cocada, or guaraná candies travel well and are easy to share. Shelf-stable, no-fridge-needed treats are ideal for an office.

gifts.title: A small bottle of cachaça
gifts.note: A miniature of good cachaça (e.g. for a team to try) is a fun, distinctly Brazilian gift for adults — modest in size so it doesn't feel like an obligation.

gifts.title: Something from your region / Unicamp
gifts.note: A small handicraft or a token representing Campinas/Unicamp adds a personal, thoughtful touch and gives you a story to tell.

culture.name: German Culture
culture.intro: The unwritten rules and everyday culture that help you read the room at work and in daily life.

items.title: Punctual & planned
items.note: Meetings start exactly on time and follow an agenda. Decisions are made thoroughly ('Gründlichkeit') rather than quickly — being well-prepared earns respect.

items.title: Direct & structured
items.note: Communication is clear and to the point; disagreement is normal and not personal. Say what you mean, back it with reasoning, and people will trust you.

items.title: 'Mahlzeit!'
items.note: Around midday in offices and canteens, colleagues greet each other with 'Mahlzeit!' (literally 'mealtime'). Just say it back — it's a friendly lunchtime hello.

items.title: Feierabend is sacred
items.note: When the workday ends, it ends. Evenings, weekends and your ~30 days of holiday are protected. Don't expect (or send) work emails after hours.

items.title: Bread is serious
items.note: Germany has hundreds of bread types and a bakery ('Bäckerei') on every corner. A cold supper of bread, cheese and cold cuts ('Abendbrot') is a classic evening meal.

items.title: Water comes sparkling
items.note: Order 'Wasser mit Gas' (sparkling) or 'ohne Gas' (still). Tap water ('Leitungswasser') is rarely served in restaurants — bottled is the norm and you pay for it.

items.title: Beer & the Reinheitsgebot
items.note: The 1516 'beer purity law' still shapes German brewing pride. Regions have their own styles — try the local one and toast with eye contact.

items.title: You bring your own cake
items.note: On your birthday, you bring cake or treats for your colleagues — not the other way around. A nice way to break the ice in a new team.

items.title: Quiet hours (Ruhezeit)
items.note: Expect quiet roughly 22:00–06:00 and all day Sunday: no drilling, vacuuming or loud music. It's law in many buildings, not just courtesy.

items.title: Privacy matters
items.note: Germany is strict about data and privacy (it shaped the EU's GDPR). Ask before photographing people, and don't be surprised by cash-first, low-tracking habits.

items.title: Watch the holidays
items.note: On public holidays ('Feiertage') almost everything closes, like a Sunday. Saxony even has its own holiday, Buß- und Bettag in November — check a calendar so a closed supermarket doesn't catch you out.

items.title: Tschüss vs. Auf Wiedersehen
items.note: 'Auf Wiedersehen' is the formal goodbye; 'Tschüss' is the everyday casual one. In the south you'll also hear 'Servus'; in the north 'Moin'.

leipzig.name: Leipzig
leipzig.intro: Your home base. A green, creative boomtown in Saxony — Bach's city, a hero of 1989, and a hub for Germany's shift away from coal (right up DBFZ's alley).

items.title: Saxony's largest city
items.note: Leipzig is the biggest city in Saxony (though Dresden is the state capital). It's booming and creative — locals half-jokingly call it 'Hypezig' or 'the new Berlin'.

items.title: City of the Peaceful Revolution
items.note: The Monday Demonstrations at the Nikolaikirche in 1989 ('Wir sind das Volk' — 'We are the people') helped bring down the Wall. Leipzig is proud to be the 'Heldenstadt' (City of Heroes).

items.title: A giant Hauptbahnhof
items.note: Leipzig's main station is one of Europe's largest by floor area — a sightseeing-and-shopping destination in itself, and 1h10–1h15 to Berlin by ICE.

items.title: Where DBFZ sits
items.note: The Deutsches Biomasseforschungszentrum is in the northeast of the city (Torgauer Straße area), reachable by tram/bus. It's a federal research centre for biomass and bioenergy.

items.title: Coal country going green
items.note: Leipzig sits in the Central German lignite mining district. The 'Strukturwandel' (structural shift away from coal) makes the region a living lab for bioenergy — great context for your research and small talk.

items.title: Lakes from old mines
items.note: South of the city, former open-pit coal mines have been flooded into the 'Neuseenland' lakes (e.g. Cospudener See). A vivid, local example of post-coal transformation — and a lovely weekend swim spot.

items.title: Bach's Thomaskirche
items.note: Johann Sebastian Bach was cantor at St. Thomas Church, where the famous Thomanerchor boys' choir still sings. The Gewandhaus orchestra is world-class, and Wagner was born here.

items.title: Spinnerei in Plagwitz
items.note: A former cotton mill turned art complex, home to the acclaimed 'New Leipzig School' (Neo Rauch). The canal-laced Plagwitz/Karl-Heine area is the creative quarter.

items.title: Völkerschlachtdenkmal
items.note: The colossal Monument to the Battle of the Nations marks the 1813 defeat of Napoleon at Leipzig. Worth the climb for the view.

items.title: Gose, the local sour beer
items.note: Leipzig's traditional 'Gose' is a slightly sour, salty wheat beer — try it at a historic 'Gosenschänke'. Saxons are also historic coffee-lovers ('Kaffeesachsen').

items.title: Leipziger Lerche
items.note: A sweet shortcrust pastry with marzipan and jam, named after a banned songbird dish. A charming local treat to bring back to the office.

items.title: 'Karli' & Auerbachs Keller
items.note: Karl-Liebknecht-Straße ('Karli') in the Südvorstadt is the buzzy bar-and-restaurant street. For history, dine at Auerbachs Keller, the cellar restaurant featured in Goethe's 'Faust'.

berlin.name: Berlin
berlin.intro: The capital, ~1h15 away by fast train — an easy weekend. International, creative and steeped in 20th-century history. English gets you far here.

items.title: Capital & a city-state
items.note: Berlin is both the national capital and its own federal state. It's famously 'arm aber sexy' (poor but sexy) — less polished than Munich, but endlessly creative and welcoming to newcomers.

items.title: Getting around (BVG)
items.note: U-Bahn, S-Bahn, trams and buses share one ticket; the U-Bahn runs all night on weekends. Most central sights are in fare zones A/B; airport BER is in zone C. Validate your ticket.

items.title: Spätis & late life
items.note: Late-night corner shops ('Spätis') are a Berlin institution for snacks and drinks when supermarkets are shut. The city stays open late — and Sundays revolve around brunch and flea markets.

items.title: The Wall's traces
items.note: See the open-air East Side Gallery (painted Wall murals), the sobering Berlin Wall Memorial at Bernauer Straße, and Checkpoint Charlie. The Brandenburg Gate is the reunification symbol.

items.title: Reichstag & Museum Island
items.note: Climb the Reichstag's glass dome (free, but book ahead). UNESCO-listed Museum Island holds the Nefertiti bust and more — note the Pergamon Museum's main hall is closed for a long renovation, so check before you go.

items.title: Memorials of conscience
items.note: The Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe and the Topography of Terror confront the Nazi era directly. Visited respectfully, they're among the most moving sites in Europe.

items.title: Kreuzberg & Neukölln
items.note: Multicultural, street-art-covered and full of nightlife and great cheap eats. The heart of alternative Berlin and its huge Turkish-German community.

items.title: Friedrichshain
items.note: Clubs and the RAW-Gelände (a former rail yard turned party complex). Gritty, young and loud — the engine room of Berlin's nightlife.

items.title: Prenzlauer Berg & Mitte
items.note: Prenzlauer Berg is leafy, café-filled and family-friendly; Mitte is the central, sightseeing core. Charlottenburg in the west is more classic and upscale.

items.title: Currywurst & Döner
items.note: Two Berlin street-food icons: currywurst (sausage with curry-ketchup) and the döner kebab, which was popularised here. Cheap, everywhere, and genuinely good.

items.title: Ask for a 'Pfannkuchen'
items.note: The jam doughnut the rest of Germany calls a 'Berliner', Berliners themselves call a 'Pfannkuchen'. Order it that way for instant local credibility.

items.title: Club culture (handle with care)
items.note: Berlin's techno scene is UNESCO-recognised. Clubs like Berghain have strict doors and a firm no-photos rule — phones away, be relaxed and respectful, and go late.
